question.text: Per SEBI's definition in the AIF Regulations (as cited in NISM Chapter 2.3.3), a hedge fund is:

answer.text: An Alternative Investment Fund which employs diverse or complex trading strategies and invests and trades in securities having diverse risks or complex products including listed and unlisted derivatives.
Any mutual fund that uses short-selling as its principal investment strategy.
A Category I AIF that invests exclusively in distressed or defaulted corporate debt.
A Category II AIF restricted from using any leverage at fund level.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Chapter 2.3.3, SEBI defines a hedge fund as 'an Alternative Investment Fund which employs diverse or complex trading strategies and invests and trades in securities having diverse risks or complex products including listed and unlisted derivatives'. Hedge funds sit in Category III because of their ability to go long/short and use fund-level leverage. The Trap: Option B confuses mutual funds with AIFs — short-selling MFs don't exist in Indian regulation. Option C conflates distressed-debt funds (Cat II SSF) with hedge funds. Option D contradicts the core feature — hedge funds specifically use fund-level leverage, which is a defining Cat III characteristic. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-B (Cat III Distributor) tests this from sales angle. XIX-C reframes for the manager — fund-level leverage, short positions, tax pass-through absence. Manager's Pro-Tip: When filing the PPM for a Cat III hedge fund, your 'investment strategy' section should map directly to the three SEBI-identified features: (a) diverse asset classes, (b) complex strategies, (c) long/short with fund-level leverage. Missing any one invites a SEBI query on why you need Cat III status.
